question: Compared with a high-aspect-ratio wing using the same section, a low-aspect-ratio wing has:

options.text: A steeper slope and a higher CLmax
A steeper lift-curve slope and a lower stalling angle
A shallower lift-curve slope and a higher stalling angle
The same slope and stalling angle, since the wing's planform is what sets the lift-curve slope and the section alone decides the stalling angle

explanation: Lower A → larger α_i per unit CL, so a = a₀/(1 + a₀/(πA)) is smaller. The wing reaches the section's stalling α_eff only at a higher geometric α. CLmax is similar or slightly lower.

question: On an untwisted rectangular wing, the stall begins:

options.text: At the root
At the tips
At mid-semi-span
Simultaneously across the span

explanation: Downwash is strongest near the tips of a rectangular wing, so local α_eff and cl are highest at the root. The root reaches clmax first; separation at the root gives buffet on the tail and preserves aileron effectiveness.

question: A strongly tapered wing (taper ratio about 0.2) without twist has:

options.text: No tendency, since taper affects only drag and the section lift is therefore identical from the root out to the tip along the full span of the wing
No tendency, since taper affects only drag
A root-stall tendency, because the root chord is largest
A tip-stall tendency, because local cl peaks near the tips

explanation: Decreasing chord with nearly elliptical load requires higher local cl outboard: cl ∝ loading/chord. Tip sections also operate at lower Re, reducing local clmax. Stall begins outboard, with roll-off and loss of aileron effectiveness.

question: Aerodynamic washout is produced by:

options.text: Adding dihedral, which tilts the wing and so changes the incidence of every section along the span by an equal amount at all points of the wing
Increasing camber toward the tip
Increasing geometric incidence toward the tip
Tip sections with less camber (zero-lift angle closer to zero) than root sections

explanation: A less-cambered tip produces less lift at the same geometric incidence (smaller α − α₀), which has the same effect as a geometric twist of α₀,root − α₀,tip.

question: A swept-back wing tends to stall first at the tips because:

options.text: Sweep moves the aerodynamic centre forward
Spanwise flow thickens the outboard boundary layer and the inboard wing induces upwash on the tips
Tips operate at higher Reynolds number
Tips operate at higher Reynolds number, which makes the tip boundary layer thicker and so causes it to separate sooner than the root in every case

explanation: The spanwise pressure gradient drives low-energy boundary-layer air outboard, thickening it at the tips. The swept geometry loads the outer panels. Tip stall moves the centre of lift forward and produces pitch-up.

question: Within about one span of the ground, a wing at constant angle of attack experiences:

options.text: Increased downwash and induced drag
No change in lift or drag, because the ground only alters the flow over the tail and has no measurable influence on the wing itself at any height
Reduced downwash and induced drag, and an increased lift-curve slope
Reduced lift and increased induced drag

explanation: The ground constrains the vertical velocity of the trailing vortex system (image vortices), reducing downwash. α_eff rises toward α, raising CL for a given α and lowering CD,i. The reduced downwash at the tail also reduces the tail download, producing nose-down pitch.
